\section[l'orgoglio]{l'orgoglio — pride}

\label{lesson:IT-C478-orgoglio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for regret, then the Italian for remorse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'orgoglio}
\textbf{l'orgoglio} — \textquotedblleft{}pride\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mio padre parla con orgoglio del suo lavoro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My father speaks with pride about his work.}
\end{quote}

The adjective is \emph{orgoglioso}; it can be good or bad, like English \emph{pride}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{orgoglio} comes from Frankish \emph{urgol} \textquotedblleft{}pride\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), a Germanic word, probably through Old French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'orgoglio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'orgoglio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{l'orgoglio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for regret, then the Italian for remorse, then say \emph{l'orgoglio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does l'orgoglio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Pride\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vergognarsi]{vergognarsi — to be ashamed, to be embarrassed}

\label{lesson:IT-C478-vergognarsi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for remorse, then the Italian for pride.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vergognarsi}
\textbf{vergognarsi} — \textquotedblleft{}to be ashamed, to be embarrassed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi vergogno di cantare davanti agli altri.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am embarrassed to sing in front of other people.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Vergognarsi di} + noun or infinitive. The noun is \emph{la vergogna}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vergognarsi} is built on \emph{vergogna} \textquotedblleft{}shame\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{verēcundia} \textquotedblleft{}modesty, shame\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{verērī} \textquotedblleft{}to respect, to fear\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vergognarsi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vergognarsi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{vergognarsi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for remorse, then the Italian for pride, then say \emph{vergognarsi} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does vergognarsi mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To be ashamed, to be embarrassed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[l'imbarazzo]{l'imbarazzo — embarrassment; awkwardness}

\label{lesson:IT-C478-imbarazzo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for pride, then the Italian for to be ashamed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'imbarazzo}
\textbf{l'imbarazzo} — \textquotedblleft{}embarrassment; awkwardness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Per l'imbarazzo non sapevo cosa dire.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I was so embarrassed I did not know what to say.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Mettere in imbarazzo} — to embarrass. \emph{Imbarazzato} — embarrassed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{imbarazzo} comes from Spanish \emph{embarazo} \textquotedblleft{}hindrance\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on a word for a bar or barrier: at first it meant an obstacle.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'imbarazzo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'imbarazzo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{l'imbarazzo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for pride, then the Italian for to be ashamed, then say \emph{l'imbarazzo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does l'imbarazzo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Embarrassment; awkwardness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[l'invidia]{l'invidia — envy}

\label{lesson:IT-C478-invidia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to be ashamed, then the Italian for embarrassment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'invidia}
\textbf{l'invidia} — \textquotedblleft{}envy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nella sua voce c'era un po' di invidia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There was a little envy in his voice.}
\end{quote}

The adjective is \emph{invidioso}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{invidia} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{invidia} \textquotedblleft{}envy, ill will\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{invidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to eye with ill will\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{vidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to be ashamed, then the Italian for embarrassment, then say \emph{l'invidia} again

\section[invidiare]{invidiare — to envy}

\label{lesson:IT-C478-invidiare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for embarrassment, then the Italian for envy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: invidiare}
\textbf{invidiare} — \textquotedblleft{}to envy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ti invidio: vai in vacanza al mare!
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I envy you: you are going on holiday to the seaside!}
\end{quote}

\emph{Invidiare qualcosa a qualcuno}: \emph{gli invidio la casa} — I envy him his house.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{invidiare} is built on \emph{invidia} \textquotedblleft{}envy\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{invidia} (Lewis \& Short), and so goes back to \emph{vidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{invidiare}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{invidiare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for embarrassment, then the Italian for envy, then say \emph{invidiare} again
\end{itemize}

(\textbf{ingenuo}.) Sly? (\textbf{furbo}.) To admire? (\textbf{ammirare}.) Mood? (\textbf{l'umore}.) Calm? (\textbf{sereno}.) Moody? (\textbf{lunatico}.) To get irritated? (\textbf{innervosirsi}.) To huff? (\textbf{sbuffare}.) Fright? (\textbf{lo spavento}.) To get frightened? (\textbf{spaventarsi}.) Panic? (\textbf{il panico}.) Relief? (\textbf{il sollievo}.) To calm down? (\textbf{tranquillizzarsi}.) To disappoint? (\textbf{deludere}.) Disappointment? (\textbf{la delusione}.) To comfort? (\textbf{consolare}.) Crying? (\textbf{il pianto}.) To sob? (\textbf{singhiozzare}.) Nostalgia? (\textbf{la nostalgia}.) Melancholy? (\textbf{la malinconia}.) To miss? (\textbf{rimpiangere}.) Regret? (\textbf{il rimpianto}.) Remorse? (\textbf{il rimorso}.) Pride? (\textbf{l'orgoglio}.) To be ashamed? (\textbf{vergognarsi}.) Embarrassment? (\textbf{l'imbarazzo}.) Envy? (\textbf{l'invidia}.) To envy? (\textbf{invidiare}.)
